plan.contextChunk: This figure is a line graph with two smooth curves showing how the equilibrium composition of a two-isomer mixture depends on the energy difference between the isomers. The plotting field is pale blue with a faint grid. The vertical axis is labeled Percent and runs from 0 to 100 with labels every 20 units. The same horizontal variable is given two scales: the bottom axis, labeled Energy difference (kJ/mol), extends from 0 to 15 with labeled ticks at 5, 10 and 15, while the top axis, labeled Energy difference (kcal/mol), covers 0 to just over 3 with ticks at 0, 1, 2 and 3. Both curves originate together at 50 percent where the energy difference is zero. The blue curve, tagged by a curved leader line to the label More stable isomer, rises steeply at small energy differences and then flattens, passing roughly 90 percent near 6 kJ/mol and approaching 100 percent at the right edge. The magenta curve, similarly tagged Less stable isomer, is its mirror image, dropping steeply and then leveling out at a few percent. The two curves add to 100 at every horizontal position, so a vertical slice anywhere on the plot reads off the population split for that energy gap. The graph attaches numbers to the relationship between a modest energy separation and a strongly lopsided equilibrium mixture.

interactionPlan.concept: A small energy difference between two isomers can produce a strongly unequal equilibrium mixture, with the more stable isomer becoming increasingly dominant as the energy gap grows.

demo_steps.title: Equal energy means equal amounts
demo_steps.narration: At zero energy difference, neither isomer is favored. The vertical guide begins where both curves meet at 50 percent, so the mixture is evenly split.

demo_steps.title: A modest gap strongly favors one isomer
demo_steps.narration: Drag the energy difference to about 5–6 kJ/mol. The blue curve is already near 90 percent while the magenta curve is near 10 percent, showing how quickly equilibrium becomes lopsided.

demo_steps.title: The two curves are complementary
demo_steps.narration: Move farther right and watch the readout: the more-stable and less-stable percentages always sum to 100. One curve rises by exactly the amount the other falls.

demo_steps.title: Same slice, different unit
demo_steps.narration: Switch the readout to kcal/mol. The vertical guide stays in the same physical place on the graph and the percentages do not change; only the numerical unit label for the energy gap changes.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Equilibrium composition responds exponentially to energy difference, so a few kJ/mol can turn a 50:50 mixture into one dominated by the more stable isomer.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the original as a clean two-axis line graph with a pale blue plot area and subtle gray grid. Use a bright blue upper curve labeled 'More stable isomer' and a magenta lower curve labeled 'Less stable isomer'; both start at 50 percent at zero energy difference, then approach 100 and 0 respectively as energy difference increases. The bottom axis should be in kJ/mol from 0 to 15, and the top axis should show the corresponding kcal/mol scale from 0 to a little above 3. The slider should place a vertical guide at the selected x-value, with colored point markers on both curves and a small readout showing energy in the selected unit plus the two percentages.

authoredContext:
You might recall from your general chemistry course that it’s possible to calculate the percentages of two isomers at equilibrium using the equation ΔE = –RT ln K, where ΔE is the energy difference between isomers, R is the gas constant [8.315 J/(K·mol)], T is the Kelvin temperature, and K is the equilibrium constant between isomers. For example, an energy difference of 7.6 kJ/mol means that about 95% of methylcyclohexane molecules have an equatorial methyl group at any given instant while only 5% have an axial methyl group. The figure plots the relationship between energy and isomer percentages.

A plot of the percentages of two isomers at equilibrium versus the energy difference between them. The curves are calculated using the equation ΔE = −RT ln K.

A graph of percent against energy difference in kilojoules per mole plots an increasing curve for more stable isomer and decreasing curve for less stable isomer.

The energy difference between axial and equatorial conformations is due to steric strain caused by 1,3-diaxial interactions. The axial methyl group on C1 is too close to the axial hydrogens three carbons away on C3 and C5, resulting in 7.6 kJ/mol of steric strain (the figure).

discrepancies: The generated default view adds a dashed vertical guide line, two colored point markers, and a white percentage readout box at x = 0, none of which appear in the source and which clutter the left side of the plot.
The source has horizontal gridlines at every 10 percent interval, while the generated plot only shows the major 20 percent gridlines.
The curve labels have semi-transparent background rectangles behind them, whereas the source labels sit directly on the pale blue plotting field.

The interactive readout box overlaps the plotted region and partially changes the visual emphasis of the original static figure, which contains only the two curves, axes, labels, grid, and leader arrows.
evaluation.notes: The main axes, dual energy scales, complementary blue/magenta curves, labels, and leader arrows are well matched, but the default interactive guide/readout and missing 10-percent gridlines prevent it from being a clean drop-in replacement.
action_items: Add minor horizontal gridlines at 10, 30, 50, 70, and 90 percent to match the source figure.
Hide the dashed guide line, colored markers, and readout box in the initial default state, or make them appear only after the user moves the slider.
Remove or greatly reduce the visible label background rectangles so the curve labels resemble the source more closely.
If keeping the readout box, reposition it so it does not obscure the plotted curves or dominate the left side of the graph.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction plan are correct, but the remaining issues are concrete rendering refinements: extra default guide/readout elements, missing 10-percent gridlines, and label background styling.
